notes: On 1 Jan 1970 Liechtenstein is governed by the FBP-VU grand coalition (since 1938) under Head of Government Gerard Batliner (FBP): FBP in ruling slot 1, VU in coalition slot 2, both as in MD with their MD sprites. The VU wins the election of 1 Feb 1970 and Alfred Hilbe takes over, which is left to the simulation (no date switch). The Christian Social Party (1961-1974) sits in 3; Catholic Church in 14; Hereditary Prince Hans-Adam's circle in 13; Security Corps (the only armed body) in 22; House of Liechtenstein in 23 with the royal crest sprite. Islamic slots are tiny immigrant/financial circles.

0.name: Die starke Hand
0.text:
The Strong Hand is a circle of senior officials, police officers and conservative notables in Vaduz who believe that the Prince's emergency powers under the 1921 constitution, not party bargaining in the Landtag, are the true safeguard of the state. Many come from families who remember the Nazi putsch attempt of 1939 and the confiscation of the princely estates in Czechoslovakia in 1945.

They see communism and the student revolt as twin threats, want long-haired agitators and foreign troublemakers expelled, and favour rule by princely decree in any crisis. Their model is order on the Swiss and West German pattern, firmly inside the Western camp. Their leverage lies in the administration, the Security Corps and the respect commanded by the throne.

1.name: Fortschrittliche Bürgerpartei
1.text:
The Progressive Citizens' Party was founded in 1918 by conservative notables loyal to the Prince and close to the Catholic Church, and it has led every Liechtenstein government since 1928. Since 1938 it has shared power with the Patriotic Union in a grand coalition, and since 1962 Gerard Batliner, a young lawyer, has been Head of Government. It faces the voters again on 1 February 1970 with a narrow majority in the fifteen-member Landtag.

The FBP stands for the monarchy, Catholic values, the customs and currency union with Switzerland and the low taxes on which the booming trust business and industry depend. It modernises cautiously and guards the balance between Prince and people. Its leverage lies in four decades of control of the administration and patronage.

2.name: Vaterländische Union
2.text:
The Patriotic Union was formed in 1936 by merging the Christian-Social People's Party of Wilhelm Beck, a leading author of the 1921 constitution, with the Liechtenstein Homeland Service, an authoritarian-leaning movement of the early 1930s. Junior partner in the coalition since 1938, it is represented in government by Deputy Head of Government Alfred Hilbe and hopes to end the FBP's long dominance at the election of 1 February 1970.

The VU combines loyalty to the Prince with a more social and reform-minded profile, appealing to employees, commuters and small business with promises of better social insurance, housing and modern infrastructure. It supports close ties with Switzerland and a cautious opening to Europe. Its leverage lies in its strength among wage earners and its share of coalition patronage.

3.name: Christlich-Soziale Partei
3.text:
The Christian Social Party was founded in 1961 to break the duopoly of the two old parties. In 1962 it won 10.1 percent but no seat, and its appeal led the Constitutional Court to strike down the 18 percent threshold; yet with 8.7 percent in 1966 it again failed to enter the Landtag under the small two-district system, and its support is now waning.

The party appeals to employees and people of modest means with Catholic social teaching: fair wages, workers' housing, better social insurance and a fairer electoral law, and an end to the patronage of the coalition partners. Loyal to the Prince and anti-communist, it is the only voice outside the grand coalition. Its leverage lies in discontent with the closed two-party system.

4.name: Compagni di Schaan
4.text:
The Comrades of Schaan are Italian workers in the factories and building sites of Schaan, Vaduz and Triesen who carry party cards of the Italian Communist Party or sympathise with the left-wing Free Italian Colonies across the Rhine in Switzerland. They read l'Unità, collect money for Vietnam and meet in back rooms, careful never to draw the attention of the authorities, who can withdraw residence permits at will.

They want trade union rights for foreign workers, equal pay, family reunification and an end to the seasonal worker system, and look to the Soviet Union and the socialist camp as the future. Liechtenstein's notables regard them as a dangerous foreign element. Their leverage lies in their place in the workforce and in PCI organisation.

5.name: Die Achtundsechziger
5.text:
The Sixty-Eighters are young Liechtensteiners studying in Zurich, Fribourg, Innsbruck and Vienna who came home from the student revolt of 1968 and the Zurich riots of that summer with long hair, Marcuse and a contempt for the cosy world of their parents. They gather in cafés and youth groups in Vaduz and Schaan and test the patience of priests and police.

They denounce the monarchy as feudal, the trust business as a laundromat for the world's capital, the exclusion of women from the vote and the Vietnam War. They want direct democracy from below, workers' self-management and solidarity with the Third World, and reject Moscow as much as Washington. Their leverage lies in provocation and a generation restless with tradition.

6.name: Hüter der alten Ordnung
6.text:
The Guardians of the Old Order are pious farmers, village notables and conservative priests who feel the ground shifting beneath them: the Second Vatican Council has changed the Mass, factories and trust offices have replaced fields, and the debate on women's suffrage, due to be put to the male voters, threatens the order of the family. They gather around the parish, the pilgrimage and the conservative Catholic press.

They reject Western permissiveness, American films and rock music, consumerism and secular liberalism, and want Church teaching to shape law and education. They would rather see Liechtenstein poor and devout than rich and godless. Their leverage lies in the villages, in the votes of older men and in the authority of the clergy.

7.name: Die Ost-Anstalten
7.text:
Among the thousands of letterbox companies registered in Vaduz, a discreet number serve the state trading organisations of the Soviet bloc. Through Liechtenstein Anstalten and foundations, Eastern buyers acquire Western machinery and electronics that the embargo lists forbid and park hard currency beyond the reach of Western courts, while a few trustees earn handsome fees and ask no questions.

The circle wants absolute secrecy, minimal regulation and a neutrality that does not take sides in East-West trade, and would gladly see Liechtenstein normalise its relations with Czechoslovakia and the Eastern bloc. Its Eastern clients answer to ministries in Moscow, Prague and East Berlin. Its leverage lies in money, the confidentiality of the trust laws and the indifference of the authorities.

8.name: Tujjar al-Mahjar
8.text:
The Merchants of the Mahjar are Lebanese Shia traders who made fortunes in diamonds, produce and commerce in Sierra Leone, the Ivory Coast and Senegal, and who keep part of their wealth in Liechtenstein foundations administered by trustees in Vaduz. Their visits to the principality are brief and discreet, but their money and their sympathies reach back to Jabal Amil in southern Lebanon.

They support Imam Musa al-Sadr, chosen in 1969 to head Lebanon's new Supreme Islamic Shia Council, and his demand for schools, development and a fair share of power for the neglected Shia community. They favour reform through education and commerce rather than revolution. Their leverage lies in capital, family trading networks and the discretion of Liechtenstein's trust law.

9.name: Halqe-ye Qom
9.text:
The Qom Circle is a handful of young Iranian technicians and trainees working in the precision and machine-tool firms of the Rhine valley, who meet to pray and read the declarations of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965. They keep apart from the leftist Iranian student groups in Zurich and Vienna and send their religious dues home to the clerics of Qom.

They want the Shah replaced by an Islamic government under the guidance of the clergy, and they denounce his alliance with the United States and Israel as well as godless communism. Watched by informers of the SAVAK, they have no influence in Liechtenstein. Their leverage lies in their devotion and their links to the clerical opposition in Iran.

10.name: Die Golfstiftungen
10.text:
The Gulf Foundations are the family foundations and Anstalten through which members of the Saudi, Kuwaiti and other Gulf ruling houses and their merchant allies hold part of their growing oil wealth in Liechtenstein. Their Vaduz trustees, bankers and lawyers form a small but well-paid lobby attentive to the wishes of distant princes who rarely set foot in the principality.

The circle stands for the conservative Sunni monarchies, their official religious establishment and their alliance with the West against communism and Arab revolution. It values discretion above all, opposes any loosening of secrecy and dislikes publicity about Muslim money. Its leverage lies in deposits, fees and the interest of Liechtenstein's financial centre in keeping such clients happy.

11.name: Hilafet Halkası
11.text:
The Caliphate Circle is a tiny group of Turkish workers in the factories of the Unterland who were touched at home by Hizb ut-Tahrir, the party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, which has also won a few followers in Turkey. Far from home, they pass around its translated booklets and meet in a worker's room after the night shift.

They want the caliphate abolished by Atatürk in 1924 restored, all Muslim lands united under Islamic law, and nationalism, secularism and both Cold War blocs swept away. They shun violence and avoid attention. Their leverage lies only in their conviction and in the party's networks among Muslim migrants in Germany and Austria.

12.name: Nur Talebeleri
12.text:
The Students of the Light are a reading circle of Turkish workers in Liechtenstein's factories who follow the teachings of Said Nursi, the Kurdish-born scholar who died in 1960 and whose Risale-i Nur commentaries inspire a vast religious movement in Turkey. They gather in a rented flat to read the Risale aloud, keeping contact with Nurcu circles among Turkish workers in Germany.

The movement seeks a faith renewed through study, reason and personal piety rather than revolution, and rejects communism and materialism. In Turkey its followers back conservative parties against the secularist establishment. Its leverage lies in discipline, mutual aid among lonely migrants and a network stretching from Istanbul to the industrial towns of Western Europe.

13.name: Kreis des Erbprinzen
13.text:
The Hereditary Prince's Circle forms around Prince Hans-Adam, born in 1945, who has completed his economics studies at St. Gallen and is starting to reorganise the princely family's finances, weakened by the loss of its Czechoslovak estates. Around him gather young economists, bankers and administrators who regard party politics in the Landtag as provincial and slow.

They want a lean, efficient state run on business principles, a strong monarch who governs as well as reigns, and a Liechtenstein that uses its sovereignty to prosper between the blocs without dependence on either camp. They see the Prince's constitutional powers as a tool for modernisation, not a relic. Their leverage lies in the dynasty, its bank and its wealth.

14.name: Katholische Kirche in Liechtenstein
14.text:
The Catholic Church is the state church of Liechtenstein under the 1921 constitution, and nearly the entire native population is Catholic. The principality forms a deanery of the Swiss Diocese of Chur under Bishop Johannes Vonderach, and the parish priests of its eleven communes remain figures of authority in schools, associations and village life, though Vatican II and prosperity are loosening their grip.

The Church defends Catholic schooling, the family, Sunday rest and Christian morality, and urges caution on divorce, mixed marriages and women's suffrage. It stands above the parties but leans conservative, is anti-communist and favours neutrality and charity toward the Third World. Its leverage lies in the pulpit, the parish associations and the Prince's own devotion.

15.name: Die Treuhänder
15.text:
The Trustees are the lawyers and fiduciaries of Vaduz who administer tens of thousands of holding companies, Anstalten and foundations for foreign clients, generating a large share of state revenue. Their pioneers include Guido Feger, who founded the Verwaltungs- und Privat-Bank in 1956, while the princely family's Bank in Liechtenstein and the state-owned Landesbank complete the financial centre.

They want absolute discretion, light regulation, minimal taxes on domiciliary companies and no foreign interference in the company law of 1926 that made the boom possible. They fund both coalition parties and regard reformers and foreign tax authorities with equal suspicion. Their leverage lies in their indispensability to public finances and their friendships at court and in government.

16.name: Die Fabrikherren
16.text:
The Factory Masters are the founders of Liechtenstein's industrial miracle: Martin Hilti, whose Schaan firm sells fastening tools across the world, the thin-film and vacuum technology company Balzers, the dental materials maker Ivoclar and a cluster of precision workshops. In a single generation they have turned a poor farming country into one of the most industrialised places in Europe.

They want low taxes, minimal regulation, free access to foreign labour and markets through the Swiss customs union and EFTA, and as little interference from politicians as possible. They distrust trade unions and the welfare ambitions of the reformers. Their leverage lies in jobs, exports and the prosperity that every voter in the principality now takes for granted.

17.name: Hüter des Riets
17.text:
The Guardians of the Riet are teachers, naturalists, birdwatchers and hunters who fight to save the Ruggeller Riet, the last great fen of the Liechtenstein Rhine valley, from drainage and building. In European Conservation Year 1970 they also warn against uncontrolled gravel extraction from the Rhine bed, the spread of houses and factories across the valley floor and new ski lifts in the mountains above Malbun.

They want nature reserves, planning laws and limits on unchecked growth, and argue that prosperity is worthless if the landscape is destroyed. They stand outside the parties and the blocs. Their leverage lies in the respect commanded by local naturalists and the growing unease of villagers watching their fields disappear.

18.name: Liechtensteinischer Arbeitnehmerverband
18.text:
The Liechtenstein Employees' Association, founded in 1920 as a workers' association, is the principality's only trade union. It represents factory, construction and office workers in a country where industry now employs most of the workforce, much of it foreign or commuting daily from Austria and Switzerland, and it negotiates collective agreements with the employers' organisations.

The union fights for higher wages, shorter working hours, better social insurance and pensions and decent housing for working families, while worrying that cheap foreign labour weakens its members' position. It is moderate, Christian-social in spirit and committed to social partnership. Its leverage lies in the labour shortage of the boom years and its links to the reform-minded wings of both parties.

19.name: Jugoslavenski klub
19.text:
The Yugoslav Club gathers construction and factory workers from Yugoslavia who have come to the Rhine valley since Belgrade opened its borders to labour emigration in the 1960s. Supported by Yugoslav consular officials in Switzerland, it organises folk evenings, football matches and language classes, and keeps its members loyal to Marshal Josip Broz Tito and the League of Communists.

Its members believe in workers' self-management and a socialism independent of Moscow, proud of Yugoslavia's leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement. They want fair wages, decent housing and the right to bring their families, and they shun both Western anti-communists and pro-Soviet hardliners. Their leverage lies in their growing numbers on the building sites.

20.name: Die Heimattreuen
20.text:
The Homeland Loyalists are Liechtensteiners alarmed that a third of the principality's residents are now foreigners, and that Swiss, Austrian, German and Italian workers, managers and their families are transforming villages that were purely local a generation ago. Inspired by James Schwarzenbach's campaign against foreign infiltration across the Rhine, they find a hearing among craftsmen, small landlords and older voters.

They demand tighter immigration quotas, priority for natives in jobs and housing, restrictions on land sales to foreigners and a halt to naturalisations. They distrust the industrialists and trustees who import labour and capital, and defend Liechtenstein's identity and sovereignty. Their leverage lies in the native electorate's fear of becoming a minority in its own country.

21.name: Die Ehemaligen
21.text:
The Old Comrades are the ageing former members of the Volksdeutsche Bewegung in Liechtenstein, the Nazi movement founded in 1938 whose putsch attempt of March 1939 aimed to bring the principality into the German Reich. Dissolved in 1945, the movement left behind men who served in the German forces, were tried after the war and returned to quiet lives in the villages.

A few still nurse the dream of a greater German community and despise democracy, Jews, communists and the Americanised West. They meet discreetly, read German far-right papers and keep contact with old comrades across the border. Their leverage is almost nil, but their existence remains an uncomfortable memory for a state proud of its loyalty to the Prince.

22.name: Fürstlich Liechtensteinisches Sicherheitskorps
22.text:
Liechtenstein disbanded its small army in 1868, and since 1933 the Princely Security Corps, a few dozen uniformed policemen based in Vaduz, has been the only armed body in the principality. Reinforced by auxiliary police in emergencies and relying on Swiss border guards under the customs treaty, it handles traffic, crime and the protection of the princely family and the government.

The Corps is loyal to the Prince and the government and has no political tradition of its own, but in a breakdown of constitutional order its commander would hold the only rifles in the country. Its officers favour order, discipline and firm action against agitators. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of force and its closeness to the throne.

23.name: Fürstenhaus Liechtenstein
23.text:
The House of Liechtenstein has ruled the principality since 1719, and Prince Franz Joseph II, reigning since 1938, was the first monarch to make Vaduz Castle his permanent home. With Princess Gina he enjoys great popularity, and Hereditary Prince Hans-Adam is preparing for the succession. Czechoslovakia confiscated the family's vast Moravian and Bohemian estates in 1945, and in 1967 the Prince sold Leonardo's Ginevra de' Benci to Washington's National Gallery.

Under the 1921 constitution the Prince shares sovereignty with the people: he appoints the government, sanctions every law and can dissolve the Landtag. The dynasty stands for Catholic tradition, neutrality and anti-communism. Its leverage lies in its constitutional powers, its wealth and the loyalty of the people.
